Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 21
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Forester
  trauma_type: Witnessed other trauma
  pcl5: 49

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Visual/Bodily Cues: Blood, Crash Discussions: Talk about accidents, Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident
  Maladaptive Strategies: Delay Sleep: stay up until very late, Avoid Reminders: Being reminded of the event by others, Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
  Memory: Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Memory Feels Alien: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me, Blocked Before Complete: I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it
  Negative Appraisals: Violated Values: I acted in ways that go against who I am, Lost Happiness: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable., Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed

Vignette:
Layla Haddad was 21 when she came for treatment, a young forester who spent most days moving between ranger roads, trailheads, and stands of pine, usually alone with a work truck, a radio, and long hours outdoors. Before the event, she described herself as easygoing and cheerful, the kind of person who liked the early quiet of the forest and did not mind the isolation. What changed began on an afternoon drive back from a field site, when she came upon the aftermath of a violent road collision on a two-lane highway bordering the land she worked on.

She had rounded a bend and seen two cars crumpled at an angle, one half in the ditch, one turned across the road. There was broken glass and a smell she still struggled to name without going quiet first: gasoline, hot metal, and blood in the heat. She pulled over and ran toward the cars. She remembered seeing blood immediately, bright and shocking against the gray road and the interior of the vehicle. She could hear someone making sounds from inside one car, and she tried to help before emergency responders arrived. In recounting it, Layla did not offer a smooth story. She would start, stop, and then seem to pull away from the scene herself, as if she could not let the memory run all the way to the end. At times she said it felt less like something that happened to her than like a clip from someone else’s life that she had somehow been forced to watch. Yet when it came close, it came with startling sensory force: if she let herself think of the road, she could suddenly smell again the mix of fuel and blood and overheated rubber, as if she were standing there.

In the weeks after, certain moments began to catch her off guard. Passing a wrecked car on the shoulder or seeing online images of cars after accidents could make her stomach drop. A small smear of blood at work—a cut hand, a scraped knee, even blood from field dressing an animal she happened upon during forestry work—could bring back the same physical jolt. Conversations were difficult too. If coworkers at the ranger station started talking about highway crashes or someone’s close call on the road, Layla would go quiet, find a reason to step out, or leave before anyone could draw her in. She told herself she just did not want to hear “all that accident stuff,” but what frightened her was how quickly her mind supplied the road, the twisted cars, the smell, the sense that she was back inside that moment.

Her work environment gave her no easy way to avoid reminders altogether. She spent much of her day driving rural roads where collisions with wildlife were common, and damaged vehicles were not unusual sights. She became increasingly vigilant behind the wheel and even while parked at trailheads. She found herself scanning constantly—checking the road shoulder, mirrors, tree line, other drivers’ speed, any hint that something was about to go wrong. If a vehicle came too fast around a curve, her whole body tightened before she had time to think. She knew the level of watchfulness was exhausting, but it felt irresponsible not to do it. After what she had seen, she was certain danger could appear without warning.

At night, sleep became something she put off. Layla stayed up very late scrolling on her phone or watching shows she barely followed because going to bed meant quiet, and quiet made room for the road to come back. She did not describe dramatic nightmares so much as a dread of lying there with the memory close by. Over time she grew worn down and irritable. The young woman who had once thought of herself as happy now said, with flat certainty, that she was “always miserable.” Friends noticed she canceled plans more often. At work she remained competent, but the long drives took more out of her, and she kept more to herself in the office when conversations drifted toward accidents, emergency response, or anything remotely similar.

Running through all of this was a painful judgment about herself. Layla had come to believe that, in those minutes on the highway, she had failed other people in the worst possible way. She should have protected them, she said, and she did not. Although others had told her she stopped, called for help, and did what she could, that did not alter her private conclusion. More than once she said that some of what she did and did not do that day went against who she was. She spoke as if the event had exposed something morally wrong in her, and this belief sat heavily beside the memory itself.

What finally brought her to seek help was a recent day at work when she passed a fresh crash scene near a forest access road and later had to sit in her truck, shaking and trying to breathe through the sudden return of the smell and images. That evening, when a coworker casually brought up local road fatalities, she left the room so abruptly that it drew attention. She came in feeling tired, ashamed, and worn thin by how much of her life had narrowed around roads, conversations, and the effort to keep the memory at bay. What she feared most was that this was now her permanent self—that the happy version of Layla was gone. What she hoped for, though she said it cautiously, was to be able to drive to work, hear ordinary conversation, and go to sleep at night without feeling that the crash was waiting for her.
